doc.title: Dave Rivello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Why he sought out Rayburn Wright, Holman and Brookmeyer
summary: What drew him to each teacher, including hearing Brookmeyer's 1980 record with Mel Lewis's band as a student in Ohio.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Nicely said. Was there something different you learned from each of your — like Brookmeyer and Bill Holman, and did you seek these people out for a specific reason?

I guess, without really thinking about it, but I sought out Bill Holman because of, you know at least with Brookmeyer and Holman — Rayburn Wright was such an incredible orchestrator and just knew how to get so many colors. Like I said, I came here only to study with him, to understand that. With Holman, with the early recordings — well not with the early recordings but the recordings when Bill wrote for the Kenton band, where it was very linear, and every once in a while you’d get a chord that was just like, oh finally, and then it would go back to being linear, and so he had a whole different approach from just the thickened line and things we were used to and shout choruses, he would just read these lines and it was very much more counterpoint oriented. And so that’s what attracted me that I wanted to know from him. And Brookmeyer just, as I said, in 1980 when he came back to Mel’s band and did the first record that he did with Mel’s band called Bob Brookmeyer Composer/Arranger, and that was after ten years of Bob not writing and being in California and lots of things. And there was a student at Youngstown State and I was there then, and he said, “You have to go to Record Oasis” or whatever it was called in the little mall there, “and you have to get this record, Bob Brookmeyer with the Mel Lewis band.” And so I went and I bought the record and I came home and I put it on and I put the needle down and I think the first track is “Ding Dong Ding” the first tune. And in like ten seconds it was like wow. Because I knew Thad’s music, I knew Gil’s music, I mean that’s what I had heard, and this was completely different in such a way that it blew my mind and I realized that this, and now I say, and many of us, Maria Schneider and Darcy Argue and people that have all studied with Bob, in that moment on that record Brookmeyer changed the whole face of large ensemble composition, single- handedly. So when I heard that I thought wow, you know, I was just a little kid from Ohio and I thought oh man it would be so amazing if someday I’d get to meet Bob Brookmeyer. Little did I know that I would spend fifteen years with him and be close with him and all those things, and the things you can’t imagine. But I wanted everything from Bob, like harmonic and melodic and just this whole sonic world of what he was doing. So I guess there were specific things but I just knew I needed something, I wanted something from these guys besides just to be around them and hear stories and know © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
what was it like working with so-and-so and how was this guy like, and so I’ve been very fortunate in my life to have those guys.
